notes.h: The EU as a trading bloc
notes.b: A trading bloc is a group of countries that remove trade barriers between themselves and act together in trade with the rest of the world.
points: The EU accounted for about 13% of world goods trade in 2024, second to China in goods; counting goods and services together, the EU is the world's largest trader, with China and the USA as the other two of the three largest.
Customs union: completed on 1 July 1968 (as the EEC), it removes tariffs between members and applies a common external tariff to imports from outside the EU.

notes.b: The single market, in force from 1 January 1993 and set up by the Single European Act of 1986, goes beyond the customs union.
points: It guarantees the four freedoms: free movement of goods, services, capital and people.
It removes non-tariff barriers: border checks, different national product standards and national preference in public contracts. Common standards, such as the CE mark, replace them.
The single market extends beyond the 27 members: the European Economic Area brings in Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, while Switzerland trades under bilateral agreements.
Imports are goods or services bought from abroad; exports are goods or services sold abroad.
Visible trade is trade in goods; invisible trade is trade in services.
Balance of trade: the value of exports minus the value of imports. A positive balance is a surplus; a negative balance is a deficit.
A tariff is a tax on imports; a quota is a limit on the quantity of imports allowed.
Intra-EU (internal) trade is trade between member states; extra-EU (external) trade is trade with countries outside the EU.

notes.h: Scale and main traders within the EU
notes.b: Most member states trade mainly with each other.
points: In 2024 intra-EU goods exports were about €4.0 trillion, against about €2.6 trillion of extra-EU goods exports; about three-fifths (about 60%) of members' goods exports stayed within the EU.
Germany is by far the largest intra-EU trader, with intra-EU goods exports of about €845 billion in 2024; Cyprus is the smallest, at about €1 billion.

The core of the EU, the Blue Banana from south-east England through the Benelux countries and the Rhine valley to northern Italy, together with the Paris Basin, dominates internal trade. Peripheral members such as Cyprus and Greece trade much less within the EU.

Eastern members depend most on intra-EU trade. Intra-EU trade was about 81% of Czechia's goods trade in 2024, compared with about 30% for Cyprus, because of their proximity to Germany and their integration into its supply chains.

notes.h: What is traded within the EU
points: Manufactured goods dominate: machinery, vehicles and parts, and chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Food and farm produce come next, and services such as finance, tourism and transport add to the total.
Intra-industry trade: members swap similar goods, such as cars for cars, and components cross borders several times in supply chains.

Since the 2004 enlargement the car industry has linked Germany with Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary and Poland. Volkswagen took over Škoda (Czechia) in stages from 1991 and has fully owned it since 2000. Slovakia makes more cars per head of population than any other country.
Complementary trade: greenhouse fruit and vegetables from Almería in southern Spain are trucked north to northern Europe, while northern manufactured goods flow south and east.

notes.h: Gateway ports and the Rotterdam effect
points: Rotterdam in the Netherlands is Europe's largest port and Antwerp in Belgium is the second largest; both sit at the mouth of the Rhine-Meuse-Scheldt delta.
Goods entering and leaving the single market through these ports are counted as trade with the Netherlands and Belgium, which gives both countries very large trade totals.
The Rotterdam effect: goods recorded as trade with the Netherlands may be going on to other member states.
Removal of tariffs and border controls: the customs union, the single market and Schengen border-free travel for most members cut costs and delays.

The euro: 21 countries used it from 1 January 2026, with Bulgaria the newest. Trade among them has no exchange costs or exchange-rate risk, and prices are easy to compare. The euro's history is in The complexity of regions (i).

Proximity and transport: short distances, dense motorway and rail networks, the Rhine (navigable to Basel in Switzerland), the Channel Tunnel (opened 1994), the Øresund Bridge between Copenhagen and Malmö (opened 2000), and EU-funded Trans-European Transport Networks (TEN-T).
A large, wealthy market: about 450 million people in 2024, with high incomes and broadly similar tastes.
Enlargement widened the single market: ten countries joined in 2004, Bulgaria and Romania in 2007 and Croatia in 2013. New members opened new markets and lower-cost production sites in the east.

Brexit moved the UK from internal to external partner. The UK left on 31 January 2020; the Trade and Cooperation Agreement has applied since 1 January 2021, with zero tariffs and zero quotas on qualifying goods. Trade with the UK nonetheless became more costly because of customs declarations, checks and rules-of-origin paperwork.
Common policies: the CAP and common food standards make farm and food trade easy within the EU. The CAP is covered in How the EU influences the Irish economy.
The European Commission negotiates trade for all 27 members under the Common Commercial Policy, so the EU speaks with one voice in the World Trade Organization (WTO).
All members apply the same common external tariff, so the EU bargains as one bloc rather than as 27 separate countries.

notes.h: Main external partners and the balance of trade (2024)
points: Export partners for extra-EU goods: the USA is the largest at about 21%, then the UK at about 13%, China at about 8%, Switzerland at about 7-8% and Turkey at about 4%.
Import partners for extra-EU goods: China is the largest at about a fifth (about 20-21%), then the USA at about 13-14%, the UK at about 7%, Switzerland at about 6% and Turkey at about 4%.
Overall, extra-EU goods exports were about €2.58 trillion and imports about €2.43 trillion, a goods surplus of about €150 billion.
The EU had a surplus with the USA and a large deficit with China.

notes.h: What the EU exports and imports
points: Exports: machinery and vehicles were about €1.0 trillion (about 39% of extra-EU exports); chemicals and related products, including pharmaceuticals, were about €560 billion (about 22%). Food, drink and services are also exported.
Imports: energy products, mainly oil and gas, were about 15% of EU imports by value in 2024, down from about 23% in 2022.
Imports also include raw materials, consumer electronics and other manufactured goods from China and Asia, and tropical foods such as coffee, cocoa and bananas.

notes.b: Political events change trade patterns quickly, as the change in energy imports shows.
points: Russia was a major gas supplier before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022.
Russian gas fell from about 45% of EU gas imports in 2021 to about 19% in 2024, through sanctions and the REPowerEU plan (launched May 2022).
The USA supplied almost half of EU liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports in 2024.
The EU plans to end Russian gas imports by the end of 2027.

notes.h: Trade agreements and access for developing countries
points: Trade agreements widen external trade: CETA with Canada has been provisionally applied since September 2017; the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement has been in force since February 2019; the EU-South Korea agreement has applied since 2011.
EU-Mercosur negotiations with Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay concluded in December 2024. Irish farm organisations strongly opposed the deal because of competition from South American beef.
The Lomé Convention (1975, with African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) countries) and the Cotonou Agreement (2000) gave preferential access to poorer countries.
Everything But Arms (2001) gives the least developed countries duty-free, quota-free access for all goods except arms.
Critics argue that tariffs on processed goods (tariff escalation) and past subsidised farm exports harmed producers in the developing world.

The EU-USA agreement of July 2025 capped the US tariff on most EU goods at 15%, including pharmaceuticals; Irish pharmaceutical exports to the USA are among the goods it covers. Steel and aluminium remained at 50%.
EU definitive duties on Chinese-made electric cars, from October 2024, reached up to about 35%.
In both disputes the EU acted as one bloc, so one set of duties or one deal applies to all 27 members.
The size and wealth of the single market gives the EU bargaining power in trade negotiations.
High-tech, high-value industry makes manufactured goods the main exports.
A lack of energy and some raw materials makes the EU dependent on imports, especially of fuels.
Historical and colonial links, including former colonies in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific and the Commonwealth ties of the former UK member, shaped the preferential agreements.
Globalisation: low-cost manufacturing in China and Asia draws in imports. The trading triad of the USA, the EU and the Pacific Rim is taught in Patterns in world trade, in The Global Economy.
Politics redirects trade: sanctions on Russia, US tariff disputes and Brexit each changed the direction of trade flows.

notes.h: Reading trade pie charts and tables
notes.b: Exam data questions give export and import shares for each partner. Use the invented values below only to practise the method.
points: Identify the largest partner: the biggest slice or the highest value.
Calculate a missing share: subtract the known shares from 100. Illustrative: exports to Country A 25% and Country B 15% leave 100 minus 25 minus 15 = 60% for all other partners.
Compare exports and imports with one partner. If the value sent to it is higher than the value received, the EU has a surplus with that partner; if it is lower, a deficit.

keyTerms.definition: A group of countries that remove trade barriers between themselves and act together in trade with the rest of the world.
A trading arrangement with no tariffs between members and a common external tariff on imports from outside.
A customs union that also removes non-tariff barriers and guarantees free movement of goods, services, capital and people.
The same tax on imports from outside the EU, applied by all member states.
The value of a country's exports minus the value of its imports.
A situation in which exports exceed imports, giving a positive balance of trade.
A situation in which imports exceed exports, giving a negative balance of trade.
Trade between member states of the EU, also called internal trade.
Trade between member states and countries outside the EU, also called external trade.
The exchange of similar goods between countries, such as cars for cars, often through supply chains.
The EU policy under which the European Commission negotiates trade for all member states as one bloc.
The rules that show where a good was made, so that it qualifies for preferential tariff-free trade.
Higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials, which discourages developing countries from processing their own exports.

factCards.term: EU trade: its world share and the dates of its two big steps
factCards.definition: About 13% of world goods trade in 2024, second to China in goods, and the largest trader counting goods and services. The customs union was completed on 1 July 1968; the single market began on 1 January 1993, set up by the Single European Act (1986).

factCards.term: Single market: which non-tariff barriers it removed
factCards.definition: Border checks; different national product standards; national preference in public contracts. Common standards such as the CE mark replaced them, on top of the four freedoms of goods, services, capital and people.

factCards.term: Which non-EU countries are in the single market, and how
factCards.definition: Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein through the European Economic Area (EEA). Switzerland is in neither the EU nor the EEA but trades through bilateral agreements.

factCards.term: Intra-EU trade: its scale in 2024
factCards.definition: Intra-EU goods exports were about €4.0 trillion against about €2.6 trillion of extra-EU goods exports, so about three-fifths (about 60%) of members' goods exports stayed inside the EU.

factCards.term: Intra-EU trade: biggest and smallest traders, and who depends most
factCards.definition: Germany is by far the largest (about €845 billion of intra-EU goods exports, 2024); Cyprus the smallest (about €1 billion). Intra-EU trade ran from about 30% (Cyprus) to about 81% (Czechia) of goods trade, as eastern members sit in Germany's supply chains.

factCards.term: What is traded within the EU, with a complementary-trade example
factCards.definition: Mainly manufactured goods (machinery, vehicles and parts, chemicals and pharmaceuticals), then food, plus services such as finance and tourism. Complementary trade: greenhouse vegetables from Almería, Spain, go north; manufactures go south and east.

factCards.term: EU car supply chains: the eastern example
factCards.definition: Since the 2004 enlargement car plants in Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary and Poland supply the German-centred industry. Volkswagen took over Škoda in stages from 1991, fully owning it since 2000. Slovakia makes more cars per head than any other country.

factCards.term: Gateway ports and the Rotterdam effect
factCards.definition: Rotterdam (Europe's largest port) and Antwerp (second) at the Rhine-Meuse-Scheldt delta handle goods entering and leaving the single market, so the Netherlands and Belgium show huge trade totals; goods recorded as Netherlands trade may go elsewhere.

factCards.term: Internal trade factors: barrier removal and the euro
factCards.definition: The customs union, single market and Schengen border-free travel cut costs and delays. The euro, used by 21 countries from 1 January 2026 (Bulgaria the newest), removes exchange costs and exchange-rate risk and makes prices easy to compare.

factCards.term: Internal trade factors: transport links and a wealthy market
factCards.definition: Short distances; dense motorways and rail; the Rhine, navigable to Basel; the Channel Tunnel (1994); the Øresund Bridge, Copenhagen to Malmö (2000); EU-funded TEN-T networks. About 450 million people (2024) with high incomes and similar tastes.

factCards.term: How EU enlargement changed internal trade
factCards.definition: Ten countries joined in 2004, Bulgaria and Romania in 2007 and Croatia in 2013. Each widened the single market, opening new markets and lower-cost production sites in the east, such as car assembly linked to Germany.

factCards.term: How Brexit changed EU–UK trade
factCards.definition: The UK left on 31 January 2020; transition ended 31 December 2020. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement (from 1 January 2021) has zero tariffs and quotas on qualifying goods, but customs declarations, checks and rules-of-origin paperwork make trade costlier.

factCards.term: EU's top five export and import partners for goods (2024)
factCards.definition: Exports: USA about 21%, UK about 13%, China about 8%, Switzerland about 7–8%, Turkey about 4%. Imports: China about a fifth (20–21%), USA about 13–14%, UK about 7%, Switzerland about 6%, Turkey about 4%.

factCards.term: EU balance of trade in goods (2024)
factCards.definition: Extra-EU exports about €2.58 trillion and imports about €2.43 trillion, a surplus of about €150 billion. The EU had a surplus with the USA and a large deficit with China.

factCards.term: What the EU exports outside the EU (2024)
factCards.definition: Machinery and vehicles about €1.0 trillion (about 39% of extra-EU exports); chemicals including pharmaceuticals about €560 billion (about 22%); also food, drink and services. High-tech, high-value industry explains this pattern.

factCards.term: What the EU imports, and why it depends on energy imports
factCards.definition: Energy, mainly oil and gas, about 15% of imports by value in 2024 (about 23% in 2022), because the EU lacks fuels and some raw materials; also raw materials, electronics from China and Asia, and tropical foods such as coffee, cocoa and bananas.

factCards.term: Russia and EU energy imports since 2022
factCards.definition: Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022; sanctions and REPowerEU (May 2022) cut Russian gas from about 45% of EU gas imports (2021) to about 19% (2024). The USA supplied almost half of EU LNG in 2024. The EU plans to end Russian gas by the end of 2027.

factCards.term: EU trade agreements: four named examples with dates
factCards.definition: CETA with Canada, provisionally applied from September 2017; EU–Japan agreement in force from February 2019; EU–South Korea from 2011; EU–Mercosur talks concluded December 2024, strongly opposed by Irish farm organisations over South American beef.

factCards.term: EU trade deals with developing countries, and a justice criticism
factCards.definition: Lomé Convention (1975) with ACP countries; Cotonou Agreement (2000); Everything But Arms (2001), duty-free and quota-free for the least developed countries. Critics say tariff escalation and past subsidised farm exports harmed developing-world producers.

factCards.term: Two recent EU trade disputes acting as one bloc
factCards.definition: The EU–USA deal of July 2025 capped US tariffs on most EU goods, including pharmaceuticals, at 15%; steel and aluminium stayed at 50%. EU definitive duties on Chinese-made electric cars from October 2024 reached up to about 35%.

factCards.term: Factors shaping the EU's external trade: name five
factCards.definition: Market size gives bargaining power; high-tech industry makes manufactures the main exports; lack of energy forces fuel imports; colonial links (Africa, Caribbean, Pacific) shaped preferential deals; sanctions, tariffs and Brexit redirect trade.

factCards.term: Skill: reading a trade pie chart or table
factCards.definition: Identify the largest partner (biggest slice); calculate a missing share by subtracting the others from 100 (illustrative: 25% and 15% leave 60%); compare exports and imports with one partner: more sent than received is a surplus, less is a deficit.

questions.prompt: Describe the current trading patterns of the European Union, both internal and external, and explain the factors that influence these patterns.
questions.model: Patterns: about three-fifths of EU members' goods exports stayed within the EU in 2024 (intra-EU goods exports of about €4.0 trillion against about €2.6 trillion extra-EU). Germany is by far the largest intra-EU trader, with about €845 billion of intra-EU goods exports, and the Blue Banana core dominates internal trade. Trade is largely in manufactured goods, with intra-industry trade and supply chains such as the car industry linking Germany with Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary and Poland. Externally, the USA is the largest export partner (about 21%) and China the largest import source (about a fifth). The EU had a goods surplus of about €150 billion in 2024, with a surplus with the USA and a deficit with China. The EU exports machinery and vehicles (about 39% of extra-EU exports) and chemicals including pharmaceuticals (about 22%), and imports energy, raw materials and manufactured goods from China and Asia. Factors: the single market removes tariffs and non-tariff barriers for about 450 million consumers; the euro removes exchange costs among 21 members; proximity, transport networks and the Channel Tunnel reduce costs; enlargement in 2004, 2007 and 2013 widened the market and added lower-cost production sites; Brexit moved the UK to external partner status, adding customs checks and paperwork; the Common Commercial Policy gives the EU bargaining power; the EU's dependence on imported energy shaped its gas trade, with Russian gas falling from about 45% of imports in 2021 to about 19% in 2024; trade agreements such as CETA and the EU-Japan agreement widen external trade; sanctions and tariff disputes with the USA and China redirect trade flows.

questions.prompt: Illustrative data only, with invented values. The export partners of an imaginary trading bloc are: Country A 25%, Country B 15%, Country C 10%, all other partners not labelled. Its import partners are: Country A 20%, Country B 30%, Country C 10%, all other partners not labelled. The value of exports to Country B is €15 billion and the value of imports from Country B is €30 billion. (a) Name the largest export partner. (b) Calculate the share of exports going to all other partners. (c) State whether the bloc has a surplus or a deficit with Country B, and give the amount. (d) Explain balance of trade.
questions.model: (a) Country A is the largest export partner, at 25%. (b) The share going to all other partners is 100 minus 25 minus 15 minus 10, which gives 50%. (c) The bloc has a deficit with Country B: imports of €30 billion are €15 billion more than exports of €15 billion, so the deficit is €15 billion. (d) Balance of trade is the value of exports minus the value of imports. A positive result is a surplus and a negative result is a deficit. Here, exports to Country B minus imports from Country B is 15 minus 30, which is minus €15 billion.

questions.prompt: Explain how changes in EU membership have affected EU trading patterns.
questions.model: Enlargement widened the single market. Ten countries joined in 2004, and Bulgaria and Romania in 2007. New members opened new markets for EU goods and lower-cost production sites in eastern Europe, so manufacturers such as the car industry built supply chains linking Germany with Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary and Poland. Intra-EU trade grew, as eastern members came to depend heavily on it. Brexit reduced the internal market. The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020 and became an external partner, so trade with it now crosses an external border. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement, applied from 1 January 2021, gives zero tariffs and zero quotas on qualifying goods, but customs declarations, checks and rules-of-origin paperwork raise the cost of trade. As a result the UK has become a separate external partner in the EU's trade figures, and the EU's trade with the UK is now recorded as extra-EU trade.
